title: A Verifier Taxonomy and Open Benchmark for Detectability of LLM‑Generated NetOps Failures
abstract: We preregistered, executed, and analyzed a paired confirmatory study that evaluates whether a machine‑readable verifier taxonomy plus an open synthetic benchmark can predict deterministic detectability of LLM‑generated network change proposals. Using a frozen preregistration (cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1) we generated 100 paired tasks (baseline: syntax‑only verifier exemplar; guarded: syntax+policy+reachability/stateful exemplar), produced candidate configurations with gpt‑5‑mini, and scored each condition with deterministic validator oracles. On the confirmatory task set both verifiers detected every injected failure (baseline = 100/100, guarded = 100/100; paired difference = 0.00, 95% CI [0.00, 0.00], McNemar p = 1.0). Thus, on this benchmark a stronger verifier did not increase detectability over the lightweight syntax exemplar. We report the preregistered design, deterministic execution artifacts, quantitative results, and a focused discussion of threats to validity and operational implications for verifier selection in NetOps workflows.

sections.introduction: Motivation. LLMs are being proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and network‑change planning. Prior work highlights frequent stochastic and semantic failures of generative systems and the need for verifier chains (generate→verify→repair) to ensure safe changes. Research gap. It remains unclear which classes of failures are reliably detectable by deterministic verifiers (syntax, policy, reachability, stateful emulation) versus those that remain semantic/intentual and require human judgment. Research question. Can a machine‑readable verifier taxonomy plus a public benchmark of LLM‑generated change proposals reliably characterize which failure classes are detectably deterministic and thereby guide deterministic verifier selection for NetOps workflows? Contributions. (1) A preregistered paired confirmatory study (cnd‑2026‑004‑prereg‑v1) that operationalizes a verifier taxonomy and a seeded synthetic NetOps task generator; (2) a fully deterministic execution with gpt‑5‑mini and Dockerized deterministic validators; (3) empirical evidence from N=100 confirmatory task pairs showing no detectability gain from the stronger guarded exemplar on this task set; (4) an analysis of failure modes, reproducibility artifacts, and clear limitations.
sections.related_work: Closest prior work: studies of LLMs for network configuration and IaC evaluation (NetConfEval, Mani et al.; Cloud/ IaC error taxonomies), and generate‑verify‑repair architectures for deterministic acceptance in regulated code (Cadenas 2026). Tools and methods for deterministic network verification (Minesweeper; Propane; Batfish lessons) motivate our use of symbolic/deterministic validators and stateful emulation. We position this study as an operational, preregistered experiment that measures verifier detectability per a small, public synthetic benchmark rather than a broad multi‑model leaderboard.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design. We preregistered the study (ID cnd-2026-004-prereg-v1). The confirmatory hypothesis (H2) tested whether a stronger verifier class (syntax+policy+reachability/stateful exemplar) increases deterministic detection by ≥15 percentage points over a syntax‑only baseline on a paired within‑task design (N=100 pairs). The primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. Task generation. The task bank contains publicly permissible synthetic NetOps change tasks (task families: intent_configuration_repair_v1) with deterministic seeds and required sequences (see execution manifest). Model and prompting. All candidate generation used gpt‑5‑mini (declared model in execution/model_configuration.json) with a shared initial candidate call per task (100 shared calls). Verifiers. Deterministic validator oracles (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implement syntax, policy, reachability, and stateful emulation checks; the baseline exemplar uses syntax‑only scoring rules while the guarded exemplar runs the fuller verifier stack. Execution and logging. The run was executed under adapter_family hosted_netops_gvr_v1; all calls, responses, validator traces, seeds, artifact hashes, and logs were recorded (see execution_manifest). Analysis plan. Primary analysis computed the mean within‑task difference, exact McNemar test and bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples) per preregistration; failed_call_treatment = complete_pair_primary (exclude infrastructure failures). All steps used only archived artifacts.
sections.results: Execution summary. The harness completed 200 episodes (100 paired tasks) with 100 hosted model calls (shared initial generation) and zero infrastructure failures. Primary outcome. Baseline detected = 100/100; Guarded detected = 100/100. Paired contingency table: n11=100, n10=0, n01=0, n00=0. Paired difference estimate = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Interpretation. On the preregistered confirmatory task set, the syntax‑only baseline already triggered deterministic validator violations for every included injected failure; adding policy+reachability/stateful checks produced no additional detected cases. Secondary and exploratory outputs. All per‑task validator traces, normalized configurations, and the paired_difference_figure.svg are available in the analysis artifacts (see artifact hashes).
sections.discussion: What the results mean. For this seeded synthetic benchmark and prompt/seed configuration, simple deterministic syntax checks sufficed to flag every injected failure class included in the confirmatory set. This implies that (a) many operationally important injected failures can be syntactically manifest in candidate outputs, and (b) a heavier verifier stack may not always yield marginal detectability gains if the lightweight checks already capture the injected failure signal. However, important caveats follow. Threats to internal validity. Our design used deterministic seeds, a single model (gpt‑5‑mini), and a single shared initial‑candidate generation per task; these choices produce low within‑task generation variability and may understate prompt/seed sensitivity. Construct validity. The task taxonomy limited leaf classes to syntax, policy‑violation, reachability‑break, stateful‑emulation‑failure, and ambiguous‑intent; the operational meaning of 'detected' depends on validator implementation (deterministic violation traces). External validity. The confirmatory tasks are synthetic and intentionally public; real operator change proposals, richer intents, or adversarial prompts may produce predominantly semantic failures that evade deterministic validators. Conclusion validity. The zero discordant count yields a null paired estimate; the pre‑registered power calculation assumed nonzero baseline rates and potential discordance, so the observed uniform detection demonstrates that the preregistered effect size target (≥15pp) cannot be evaluated meaningfully when both conditions saturate at 100%. Operational implications. Practitioners should (i) instrument and measure where lightweight validators already detect issues before deploying heavier verification stages, (ii) consider targeted taxonomies that include non‑syntactic semantic checks (intent alignment or operator intent verification) when syntax passes but intent is suspect, and (iii) maintain reproducible logging and deterministic validators for auditability.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired study to measure whether stronger deterministic verifier classes improve detectability of LLM‑generated NetOps failures. On the 100 confirmatory paired tasks (synthetic, seeded) both the baseline syntax validator and the guarded syntax+policy+reachability/stateful validator detected every injected failure (100/100). Therefore, for this benchmark and generation regime the stronger verifier did not increase detectability. This negative result is informative: it shows (a) that many engineered failure injections are syntactically manifest and can be caught by lightweight validators, and (b) that evaluating verifier architectures requires diverse task banks that exercise true semantic/intentual failure modes. We release all artifacts, logs, validator traces, and hashes to enable transparent reproduction and future extensions that expand model, prompt, and task diversity. Future work should evaluate (i) seed/prompt sensitivity across multiple models, (ii) adversarially crafted semantic failures, and (iii) human‑in‑the‑loop decisions for intent alignment when deterministic validators pass.

limitations: Single model and single generation pass: only gpt‑5‑mini and one shared initial candidate per task were evaluated; prompt/seed/model variability is therefore not covered by the confirmatory result.

Synthetic and public task bank: confirmatory tasks were seeded synthetic items with public provenance; real operator proposals or adversarially crafted prompts may yield different detectability patterns.

Validator implementation dependence: 'detected' depends on the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation and its canonical violation tokens; different validator designs (e.g., looser normalization, probabilistic entailment judges) may change outcomes.

Saturation effect: both conditions produced 100% detection on the confirmatory set, preventing inference about marginal gains; the preregistered effect-size target (≥15pp) could not be evaluated under saturation.
Semantic intent failures untested: the confirmatory leaf taxonomy did not exhaustively include subtle intent‑misalignment failures that might pass deterministic syntax checks.
